frames.body: {{ENTITY}} pursues a lawful, specific, and present interest in preventing fatality and serious injury to underground shift workers by detecting medical events and unauthorised zone entry in real time. This interest is real and not speculative: underground rare-earth mining carries inherent, documented risks of physical harm, and the Mines Regulations 2014 and the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 impose positive duties on the employer to manage those risks. {{CITE_1:cite}} The interest is shared by the controller and the shift workforce: supervisors gain the operational capacity to intervene, and workers gain real-time protection against foreseeable life-threatening events.

The legitimate interest in the controller's own words was not provided; the assessment relies on the stated purpose to data subjects and the processing description. The interest must be articulated with equal precision in the controller's own documentation before the LIA can be {{STAGE}}ised.

{{CITE_1:cite}} (1) Reasonable expectations — workers in underground rare-earth mining reasonably expect proportionate safety monitoring given the inherent, documented hazards of the work environment; Continuous physiological monitoring may not be expected in the abstract, but the intake states that a handbook addendum and works-council consultation were {{0_}}d before deployment, bringing the monitoring into the workers' reasonable awareness prior to processing. (2) Nature of the relationship — the employment relationship involves an inherent power imbalance, recognised as a risk factor for balancing in the employment context; however, the stated purpose is protective of the data subjects themselves, and the monitoring is tied to a high-hazard physical environment. The works-council agreement and contractual exclusion from performance management narrow the scope of the employer's power to use the data against the worker's interests. (3) Potential impact and severity — the worst-case harms identified are: (a) misuse for productivity surveillance, (b) inference of medical conditions beyond the safety purpose, and (c) a chilling effect on legitimate rest behaviour. As to likelihood: on the facts stated, the safeguards — dashboard pseudonymisation, strict purpose limitation written into the employment handbook, contractual exclusion from performance management, annual external review, and access restriction to on-call supervisor and medic on alarm — reduce the probability of safeguard failure to a level that is plausible but not foreseeable as a routine occurrence. As to severity: if safeguards were to fail, the resulting harm would be significant in nature — health data inference and productivity surveillance each engage discrimination and chilling-effect risks that are qualitatively serious for workers in a power-imbalanced employment context. (4) Safeguards including opt-out — pseudonymised dashboards, automated 90-day deletion with attestation, strict safety-only purpose written into contract, annual independent external review, works-council sign-off, and restricted re-linkage on alarm are substantial and documented.
Works-council agreement was {{0_}}d before deployment, providing collective worker representation in the decision and strengthening the reasonable-expectation analysis.

On likely impact (para. 39): the record acknowledges a worst-case harm of unexpected profiling if safeguards fail; while this is a real potential impact, it is mitigated by the described controls and is not an inherent outcome of the processing as described. The safeguards in place — {{SAFEGUARDS:list}} controls, pseudonymisation of analytics user IDs, privacy-centre preference controls, and a stated commitment to {{SAFEGUARDS_2:list}} — collectively reduce the risk that the processing causes disproportionate harm, though the absence of concrete retention figures (see necessity_test open_questions) means the adequacy of retention as a safeguard cannot be fully confirmed from the record. No vulnerable subjects are indicated, which removes a significant weighting factor against the controller. On balance, the interest in service integrity and fraud prevention, supported by a direct customer relationship and reasonable user expectations, is not overridden by the data subjects' interests on the facts provided — subject to the retention and scope gaps identified.
